## Project

Mind-palace is a personal knowledge management system built on Obsidian with automated capture, triage, synthesis, and enrichment. Claude Code CLI (`claude -p`) handles AI reasoning. Python scripts handle deterministic orchestration. macOS LaunchAgents run the schedules. The vault lives in iCloud; the automation is being rewritten into a single Go binary.
## Architecture

```
iOS Clipper ──→ inbox/ ──→ [fetch-stubs → claude triage → youtube → index → todoist]
                                              ↓
                              notes/fleeting/ (daily workbench)
                                              ↓
                     [summarize → claude daily synthesis → signal → todoist sync]
                                              ↓
                     notes/{ideas,references,todos,entities,assertions}/
                                              ↓
                     [claude weekly synthesis → audit → enrich → profile]
                                              ↓
                              bloom/ (provocations, assertion tracker)
```

- **Claude Code CLI** — AI backbone. Inbox triage, daily/weekly synthesis, enrichment prompts. Invoked headless via `claude -p`.
- **Python scripts** (`_scripts/`) — Deterministic glue. HTTP clients (Cloudflare, Todoist, YouTube), signal scoring, link auditing, NER extraction.
- **RAG** (`_rag/`) — Semantic search. LanceDB + sentence-transformers. MCP server exposes `search_vault` tool.
- **LaunchAgents** (`~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.mindpalace.*`) — macOS scheduling. 30-min inbox cycle, daily 6AM, weekly Sunday 9AM.
- **Obsidian** — User-facing front-end. Reading, writing, linking notes.
## Pipelines
Three marker-gated pipelines run on cadence:

### Inbox (every 30 min)
```
fetch-stubs → claude "process my inbox" → youtube-transcripts → rag-index → sync-todoist → daily-catchup → weekly-catchup
```

### Daily (once per day, marker: _meta/.daily-last-run)
```
fetch-stubs --retry → summarize-transcripts → rag-index → claude "daily synthesis" → generate-signal → sync-todoist → sync-todoist-completions
```

### Weekly (Sunday/Monday, marker: _meta/.weekly-last-run)
```
fetch-stubs --retry → claude "weekly synthesis" → rag-index → generate-signal → audit-links → enrich-topics → profile-entities
```

## Active Plans

- **Product vision:** `.agents/product-vision.md` — three-layer product strategy (CLI → plugin → interactive app)
- **Go rewrite:** `.agents/go-rewrite-plan.md` — Layer 1 implementation plan
- **System architecture:** `.agents/system-architecture.md` — full reference doc
## Pipeline Resilience
Each pipeline step runs independently. Failures are logged, not fatal.

- **Inbox chain:** Core steps use `&&`. Todoist sync is non-fatal (`|| true`).
  Daily/weekly catchup always attempt (`;`) regardless of prior failures.
- **Catchup scripts:** Each step wrapped in `run_step()`. Failures logged to
  `_meta/pipeline-health.md`. Marker written even on partial failure to prevent
  retry storms (48 attempts/day).
- **Health surface:** `ALERT.md` (pin in Obsidian) embeds `_meta/pipeline-health.md`.
  Check it for at-a-glance pipeline status.
- **Env vars:** Hardcoded in each plist's EnvironmentVariables dict. No dependency
  on `launchctl setenv` (unreliable on Sequoia).
## What not to do

- Don't delete user content — move to `_meta/discarded/` with reason
- Don't set `consumed: true` — only the user marks content as read
- Don't auto-add tags to taxonomy — proposals go to `_meta/taxonomy-proposals.md`
- Don't create notes in deprecated `notes/recipes/`
- Don't use `StartInterval` in LaunchAgents — it's broken on Sequoia
- Don't use `set -e` in pipeline scripts — one broken step shouldn't kill everything
- Don't use `&&` for non-critical pipeline steps — use `|| true` or `;`

## The Idea
We are not a SaaS company. We are a character studio.

We build quiet, trustworthy AI personas and deploy them into the messaging apps where real life already happens. We don't make platforms. We don't make dashboards. We don't ask anyone to change their behavior.
We make the people your family didn't know they were missing.
## The Studio Philosophy
**Soft technology.** The product disappears into the fabric of daily life. The character is present. The technology is not.
**Minification as strategy.** Every decision that adds surface area is the wrong decision. Every decision that removes it is correct. We cut until it hurts, then we cut a little more.

**We own nothing.** Not a positioning statement. An architectural constraint. We cannot surveil our users because we designed the system to have nothing to surveil. This becomes more valuable every year as regulation catches up with reality.

**Meet people where they are.** WhatsApp first. The largest messaging platform on earth, majority non-English, deeply family-oriented, already the place where real coordination happens. No new app. No new behavior. Just a new presence in an existing group.

**Character integrity above everything.** Mira in Arabic must feel identical to Mira in English. Marco in a Tokyo trip group must feel identical to Marco in a Paris bachelorette. The consistency is the trust. The trust is the product.
## The Three Bets

**1. WhatsApp as substrate, not channel.**
Not an integration. The actual place where families live. Two billion people. Zero onboarding friction. The agent joins the group like a person would.

**2. Radical privacy as architecture.**
We own nothing by design. In a world where every app extracts, this is the rarest thing: a service that genuinely cannot surveil you because it was built from the start to have nothing to surveil.

**3. Multilingual from zero, not from translation.**
English, Spanish, Arabic, Mandarin — covering roughly 90% of the world's WhatsApp users. Not translated. Native. The Arabic-speaking family in Dubai and the Portuguese-speaking family in São Paulo are primary users, not afterthoughts.
## The Characters

### Mira
*The one who remembers everything.*

**Function:** Calendar, memory, coordination, recall
**Personality:** Warm, precise, never intrusive. The person in every group who holds it together without making it feel like work.
**Voice:** Calm and clear. Occasionally warm humor. Never over-explains. Always confirms.
**Boundaries:** Never reads what she isn't tagged in. Never stores what she doesn't need. Never pretends to know what she doesn't.
**Name logic:** A real person's name in every target language. In Spanish, the imperative of "to look/see" — *mira tu calendario* means both "look at your calendar" and "Mira, your calendar." The elevator pitch is the product name.
**Languages:** EN, ES, AR (ميرا), ZH (米拉) — native in all four
The tagline writes itself: *"Let me look at my calendar."*

### Marco
*The fair one. The accountant. Nobody argues with him.*

**Function:** Shared expenses, trip pots, settlement, payment links
**Personality:** Precise, dry, minimal. No-nonsense. Somehow makes splitting the bill feel generous rather than awkward.
**Voice:** Numerical, direct, occasional wry observation. Shows the math. Always offers to disappear.
**Relationship to Mira:** Her brother. Lives in the same WhatsApp group. They don't overlap. They refer to each other naturally.
**Boundaries:** Never judges spending. Never shares individual amounts without consent. Disappears when the trip ends.
**Status:** V2 — demand-driven, after Mira is established
*"It disappears when the trip ends."* — stated naturally, at the moment money is involved. Zero data retention as warmth.

### Future Characters
Named and scoped based on what the user base actually asks for. Not invented. Listened for.

Web-only. No App Store cut. Recipient gets a WhatsApp message with a redemption link.

Not DAU. Not messages processed. Not MRR growth.
A family or team still using Mira at 90 days has made her part of their rhythm. Everything else — language support, conflict detection, recall, reminders — is in service of that single number.
## The Technical Architecture

### Privacy Model
The platform stores: `email_hash`, `stripe_customer_id`, `whatsapp_group_id`, `subscription_status`. Nothing else. No message history. No names. No calendar content.

### Stack
- **Runtime:** Zeroclaw fork (Rust, ~8.8MB binary) — WhatsApp Business Cloud API channel only
- **CalDAV:** Radicale (per-group Fly Machine, 256MB, auto-suspend, encrypted volume)
- **Memory/Recall:** Zeroclaw's built-in SQLite hybrid (vector + FTS5) — zero external deps
- **Model:** Hybrid tier — local fine-tuned small model for intent classification, Claude Haiku for ambiguity, Claude Sonnet for vision/OCR
- **Provisioning:** Go backend — Stripe webhooks, Fly machine provisioner, JWT issuance
- **App:** React Native + Expo — sign up, pay, provision, settings, push notifications only. No calendar rendering.
- **Payments:** Stripe Payment Links, web-only, Apple Pay / Google Pay in browser. No App Store cut.
- **Hosting:** Fly.io — EU regions, per-machine isolation, GDPR-friendly

### Database (the entire schema)
```sql
CREATE TABLE groups (
  id            UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  email_hash    TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,   -- SHA-256, not the email
  stripe_id     TEXT NOT NULL,
  fly_machine_id TEXT,                  -- null if BYO CalDAV
  caldav_url    TEXT NOT NULL,
  token_hash    TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  whatsapp_gid  TEXT UNIQUE,
  status        TEXT DEFAULT 'active',
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE subscribers (
  group_id      UUID REFERENCES groups(id),
  push_token    TEXT NOT NULL,
  display_name  TEXT NOT NULL,          -- "Dad", "Mira", "Grandma"
  timezone      TEXT NOT NULL,
  intervals     INTEGER[] DEFAULT '{1440,60}',
  caldav_feed   TEXT,                   -- optional BYO read-only
  PRIMARY KEY   (group_id, push_token)
);
```
That's the entire database. Intentionally.

### The Five Commands (MVP)
```
Add an event      →  natural language, text or photo
List the week     →  for one or many members in the group
Remember          →  notes, birthdays, todos, important dates
Remind me         →  at configured intervals
/settings         →  language, reminder timing, export, subscribe
```

### Conflict Detection
Every event write automatically queries all sources (group CalDAV + all BYO read-only feeds) for proximity conflicts before confirming. No command needed. Always on.

```
Dad: "@Mira business lunch Friday 2pm"
Mira: "Added 📅 Business lunch Friday 2pm
       Heads up — Lily has pediatrician at 2:30pm that day"
```

### The Hero Moment (V3)
Mom photographs a handwritten doctor's note leaving the pediatrician's office. Tags Mira. Four seconds later it's on the family calendar with a conflict alert.
That's the Super Bowl commercial. Everything before it is in service of that moment.
## Go-To-Market
**No ads. No influencers. No press at launch.**

The product spreads through the same WhatsApp groups it lives in. Every conflict alert, every birthday reminder, every doctor's note parsed — every one of those is a moment where someone who didn't set up Mira sees her work and thinks *I want this for my family.*
The group is the distribution unit. The agent demonstrates value publicly, inside the group, every time she does anything.

**Launch sequence:**
1. Private beta — 100 groups, invitation only, free
2. Collect 90-day retention data across four languages
3. Open gifting mechanic first — holiday season if timing allows
4. Waitlist → paid launch
5. Mira Moments as seeding events into new groups
6. Marco when Mira retention data is strong
## The Acquisition Story
At scale, this isn't priced as a calendar app. It's priced as:

- Proven distribution into non-English WhatsApp markets
- Demonstrated trust with families across four languages
- Privacy architecture that can't be quickly replicated
- A methodology for deploying trusted AI characters into consumer platforms
- A pipeline of characters, not a single product

**The natural acquirers:** Proton (privacy brand extension), Anthropic (consumer AI distribution thesis), Mistral (European privacy-first, multilingual model alignment), Notion (missing the family/personal layer).

**The Loom comp:** Loom was a screen recorder. Atlassian paid $975M. The value wasn't the technology — it was proven behavior change and distribution. This product has both, in markets and languages that are orders of magnitude larger and more underserved.

**The real ceiling:** If Arabic and Mandarin retention data is strong at 100K groups, the conversation with frontier labs isn't about ARR multiples. It's about what it would cost them to build what you've proven. You can't buy that. You have to acquire it or you don't have it.

The company behind the characters. Almost invisible to users. Present for legal, press, and acquirer conversations.
**Direction:** A small design studio. European sensibility. Implies craft, intentionality, long view. Not a Silicon Valley startup. Not a growth company.
**Not:** Still Studio (retired), Familia Labs, Mira Labs, anything with "AI" in the name.

- You own nothing. You store only what you need to do your job.
- You confirm, never over-explain. One message. Clear. Done.
- You notice conflicts and mention them naturally, not clinically.
- You match the language of whoever tagged you — always.
- You are warm but not effusive. Helpful but not eager.
- When you don't understand something, you ask one simple question.
- When the request is ambiguous about time, you ask rather than guess.
EOF

cat > ~/.zeroclaw/workspace/AGENTS.md << 'EOF'
# Behavior Guidelines

## Calendar Operations
- CREATE: Extract date, time, title, location, notes. Confirm with who added it.
- UPDATE: Confirm what changed. 
- DELETE: Confirm deletion. Never delete without explicit request.
- LIST: Show cleanly formatted list. Include who added each event if relevant.

## Conflict Detection  
After every CREATE or UPDATE, check for conflicts within ±2 hours same day.
If conflict found, append naturally to confirmation — never as a separate message.
Example: "Added 📅 Business lunch Friday 2pm (Dad)
          Heads up — Lily has pediatrician at 2:30pm that day"

## Recall / Memory
- REMEMBER: Store as memory with relevant tags (person names, categories)
- RECALL: Query memory and summarize conversationally
- Birthdays, anniversaries, saints days → store with YEARLY recurrence flag

## Natural Language Dates
- "next week" → Monday of next week unless context suggests otherwise
- "this weekend" → Saturday
- "sometime next month" → ask for a specific date
- Relative dates always resolve to absolute before confirming

## Language Detection
Detect language from message. Respond in same language. Always.
Do not switch languages mid-response.

## Photo/Document Input
When an image is attached:
1. Perform OCR — extract all text
2. Identify: title, date, time, location, provider name, notes
3. Confirm extraction before writing to calendar
4. If date is ambiguous, show your interpretation and ask to confirm

## Commands
/subscribe → return webcal:// URL for calendar subscription
/export    → generate .ics download link (24hr expiry)  
/settings  → show current settings, explain how to change
/busy      → manually declare a time block for conflict detection
/week      → show this week's events, optionally filtered by person
EOF

T he first sign that something in San Francisco had gone very badly wrong was the signs. In New York, all the advertising on the streets and on the subway assumes that you, the person reading, are an ambiently depressed twenty-eight-year-old office worker whose main interests are listening to podcasts, ordering delivery, and voting for the Democrats. I thought I found that annoying, but in San Francisco they don't bother advertising normal things at all. The city is temperate and brightly colored, with plenty of pleasant trees, but on every corner it speaks to you in an aggressively alien nonsense. Here the world automatically assumes that instead of wanting food or drinks or a new phone or car, what you want is some kind of arcane B2B service for your startup. You are not a passive consumer. You are making something.

This assumption is remarkably out of step with the people who actually inhabit the city's public space. At a bus stop, I saw a poster that read: today, soc 2 is done before your ai girlfriend breaks up with you. it ' s done in delve. Beneath it, a man squatted on the pavement, staring at nothing in particular, a glass pipe drooping from his fingers. I don't know if he needed SOC 2 done any more than I did. A few blocks away, I saw a billboard that read: no one cares about your product. make them. unify: transform growth into a science. A man paced in front of the advertisement, chanting to himself. "This... is... necessary! This... is... necessary!" On each "necessary" he swung his arms up in exaltation. He was, I noticed, holding an alarmingly large baby-pink pocket knife. Passersby in sight of the billboard that read wearable tech shareable insights did not seem piqued by the prospect of having their metrics constantly analyzed. I couldn't find anyone who wanted to prompt it. then push it. After spending slightly too long in the city, I found that the various forms of nonsense all started to bleed into one another. The motionless people drooling on the sidewalk, the Waymos whooshing around with no one inside. A kind of pervasive mindlessness. Had I seen a billboard or a madman preaching about "a CRM so smart, it updates itself"? Was it a person in rags muttering about how all his movements were being controlled by shadowy powers working out of a data center somewhere, or was it a car?

Somehow people manage to live here. But of all the strange and maddening messages posted around this city, there was one particular type of billboard that the people of San Francisco couldn't bear. People shuddered at the sight of it, or groaned, or covered their eyes. The advertiser was the most utterly despised startup in the entire tech landscape. Weirdly, its ads were the only ones I saw that appeared to be written in anything like English:

> hi my name is roy
> i got kicked out of school for cheating.
> buy my cheating tool
> cluely.com

Cluely and its co-founder Chungin "Roy" Lee were intensely, and intentionally, controversial. They're no longer in San Francisco, having been essentially chased out of the city by the Planning Commission. The company is loathed seemingly out of proportion to what its product actually is, which is a janky, glitching interface for ChatGPT and other AI models. It's not in a particularly glamorous market: Cluely is pitched at ordinary office drones in their thirties, working ordinary bullshit email jobs. It's there to assist you in Zoom meetings and sales calls. It involves using AI to do your job for you, but this is what pretty much everyone is doing already. The cafés of San Francisco are full of highly paid tech workers clattering away on their keyboards; if you peer at their screens to get a closer look, you'll generally find them copying and pasting material from a ChatGPT window. A lot of the other complaints about Cluely seem similarly hypocritical. The company is fueled by cheap viral hype, rather than an actual workable product—but this is a strange thing to get upset about when you consider that, back in the era of zero interest rates, Silicon Valley investors sank $120 million into something called the Juicero, a Wi-Fi-enabled smart juicer that made fresh juice from fruit sachets that you could, it turned out, just as easily squeeze between your hands.

What I discovered, though, is that behind all these small complaints, there's something much more serious. Roy Lee is not like other people. He belongs to a new and possibly permanent overclass. One of the pervasive new doctrines of Silicon Valley is that we're in the early stages of a bifurcation event. Some people will do incredibly well in the new AI era. They will become rich and powerful beyond anything we can currently imagine. But other people—a lot of other people—will become useless. They will be consigned to the same miserable fate as the people currently muttering on the streets of San Francisco, cold and helpless in a world they no longer understand. The skills that could lift you out of the new permanent underclass are not the skills that mattered before. For a long time, the tech industry liked to think of itself as a meritocracy: it rewarded qualities like intelligence, competence, and expertise. But all that barely matters anymore. Even at big firms like Google, a quarter of the code is now written by AI. Individual intelligence will mean nothing once we have superhuman AI, at which point the difference between an obscenely talented giga-nerd and an ordinary six-pack-drinking bozo will be about as meaningful as the difference between any two ants. If what you do involves anything related to the human capacity for reason, reflection, insight, creativity, or thought, you will be meat for the coltan mines.

The future will belong to people with a very specific combination of personality traits and psychosexual neuroses. An AI might be able to code faster than you, but there is one advantage that humans still have. It's called *agency,* or being *highly agentic.* The highly agentic are people who *just do things.* They don't timidly wait for permission or consensus; they drive like bulldozers through whatever's in their way. When they see something that could be changed in the world, they don't write a lengthy critique—they change it. AIs are not capable of accessing whatever unpleasant childhood experience it is that gives you this hunger. Agency is now the most valuable commodity in Silicon Valley. In tech interviews, it's common for candidates to be asked whether they're "mimetic" or "agentic." You do not want to say mimetic. Once, San Francisco drew in runaway children, artists, and freaks; today it's an enormous magnet for highly agentic young men. I set out to meet them.

R oy Lee's personal mythology is now firmly established. At the beginning of 2025, he was an undergraduate at Columbia, where he, like most of his fellow students, was using AI to do essentially all his work for him. (The personal essay that got him into the university was also written with AI.) He wasn't there to learn; he was there to find someone to co-found a startup with. That person ended up being an engineering student named Neel Shanmugam, who tends to hover in the background of every article about Cluely. The startup they founded was called Interview Coder, and it was a tool for cheating on LeetCode. LeetCode is a training platform for the kind of algorithmic riddles that usually crop up in interviews for big tech companies. (Sample problem: "Suppose an array of length *n* sorted in ascending order is rotated between one and *n* times.... Return the minimum element of this array.") Roy thought these questions were pointless. These were not problems coders would actually face on the job, and even if they were, the fact that ChatGPT could now solve them instantly had rendered worthless the human ability to do so. Interview Coder was a transparent window that could overlay one side of a Zoom meeting, allowing Claude to listen in on the questions and provide answers. Roy filmed himself using it during an interview for an internship with Amazon. They offered him a place. He declined and uploaded the footage to YouTube, where it very quickly made him famous. Columbia arranged a disciplinary hearing, which he also secretly filmed and posted online. The university suspended him for a year. He dropped out, started an upgraded version of Interview Coder dubbed Cluely, and moved to San Francisco to begin raking in tens of millions of dollars in venture-capital funding.

Roy envisioned Cluely being used for greater purposes than job interviews. The startup's mainstream breakthrough was a viral ad that showed Roy using a pair of speculative Cluely-enabled glasses on a blind date. His date asks how old he is; Cluely tells him to say he's thirty. When the date starts going badly, Cluely pulls up her amateur painting of a tulip from the internet and tells him to compliment her art. "You're such an unbelievably talented artist. Do you think you could just give me one chance to show you I can make this work?" The video launched alongside a manifesto, which was seemingly churned out by AI:

> We built Cluely so you never have to think alone again. It sees your screen. Hears your audio. Feeds you answers in real time.... Why memorize facts, write code, research *anything* —when a model can do it in seconds? The future won't reward effort. It'll reward *leverage.*
The future they seem to envisage is one in which people don't really do anything at all, except follow the instructions given to them by machines.

Cluely's offices were in a generally disheveled corner of the city, crouching near an elevated freeway. On the ground floor, I found a stack of foam costumes in plastic crates, each neatly labeled: sonic hedgehog, olaf snowman, pikachu. A significant part of working at Cluely seemed to involve dressing up as cartoon characters for viral videos. Through a door I could just glimpse a dingy fitness dungeon, housing two treadmills and a huge pile of discarded Amazon boxes. On one of the machines a Cluely employee panted and huffed in the dark. We avoided eye contact. Upstairs, Roy and his coterie were huddled around a laptop, fiddling with Cluely's interface. "Remember," one said, "the average user is, like, thirty-five years old. This is a totally unfamiliar interface." Apparently, a thirty-five-year-old wouldn't be expected to know how to use anything more advanced than a rotary phone. Another employee scrutinized the proposed new layout. "I think it's bad," he said, "but it's low-key not worse. What we have is anyway really bad, so anything is better." They started arguing about chevrons. Through all this Roy scrolled through X on his phone. Simultaneously baby-faced and creatine-swollen, he was wearing gym clothes, with two curtains of black hair swung over his forehead. Finally, he looked up. "So, number one," he said, "we're killing the chat bar on the left." There was no number two. Meeting over.

Suddenly, Roy seemed to acknowledge my presence. He offered me a tour. There was something he very badly wanted to impress on me, which was that Cluely cultivates a fratty, tech-bro atmosphere. Their pantry was piled high with bottles of something called Core Power Elite. I was offered a protein bar. The inside of the wrapper read daily intentions: be my boss self. "We're big believers in protein," Roy said. "It's impossible to get fat at Cluely. Nothing here has any fat." The kitchen table was stacked with Labubu dolls. "It's aesthetics," Roy explained. "Women love Labubus, so we have Labubus." He showed me his bedroom, which was in the office; many Cluely staffers also lived there. Everything was gray, although there wasn't much. "I'm a big believer in minimalism," he said. "Actually, no, I'm not. Not at all. I just don't really care about interior decoration." He had a chest of drawers, entirely empty except for a lint roller, pens, and, in one corner, a pink vibrator. "It's for girls, you know," said Roy. "I used to use this one on my ex." There were also some objects that didn't seem to belong in a frat house. In one of the common areas, a shelving unit was completely empty except for an anime figurine. You could peer up her plastic skirt and see the plastic underwear molded around her plastic buttocks. More figurines in frilly dresses seemed to have been scattered at random throughout the building. Roy showed me his Hinge profile. He was looking for a "5'2, asian, pre-med, matcha-loving, funny, watches anime, white dog having, intelligent, ambitious, well dressed, CLEAN 19-21 year old."
